briefing.text: The hypothesis requires a community-level income exposure (e.g. census-tract or zip-level median income, area deprivation index) measured per patient. Before modelling, search every header and every '#' description line of all provided files for income, socioeconomic, deprivation, zip, tract, county, or other geographic identifiers. Do not substitute proxies such as race, smoking, PSA or disease extent for income. If an area-level income variable is present, model it with standard errors clustered by area (or a multilevel model), because patients from the same area are not independent.
briefing.reason: Whether the exposure variable exists determines whether the claim can be tested at all, and using a proxy in its place would test a different hypothesis.

briefing.text: Self-reported RACE is a social category, not a measure of genetic ancestry. The hypothesis asks for adjustment for both race and ancestry, so look separately for a genetic-ancestry estimate (e.g. percent African/European ancestry, ancestry principal components). Do not report an ancestry adjustment when only RACE was used.
briefing.reason: This stops the team from counting a race-only model as the race-plus-ancestry adjustment that the hypothesis specifies.

briefing.text: Use the curated 8Q_ARM column in data_clinical_sample.txt as the 8q-gain outcome. If you recompute arm calls from data_cna_hg19.seg, use an arm-level rule (e.g. at least 70% of the arm covered by segments above about 0.2 log2), check agreement with the curated column, and prefer the curated column where they disagree.
briefing.reason: Calling 8q gain with a naive log2 threshold ignores purity, ploidy and panel coverage, so the outcome would be misclassified.

briefing.text: Some patients have more than one sample (e.g. T01 and T02). Count SAMPLE_ID per PATIENT_ID, then keep one sample per patient or use patient-clustered models when relating patient-level variables to 8q status.
briefing.reason: Duplicate samples inflate n and break the independence assumption.

briefing.text: The frequency of 8q gain differs strongly by sample type (metastatic vs primary), disease extent and Gleason score. In any exposure model, adjust or stratify for SAMPLE_TYPE, DISEASE_EXTENT and Gleason score.
briefing.reason: These are major confounders of any association with 8q gain.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assumed that a community-level income exposure has to be an explicit column, and that nothing in the files (an area code, an institution or site field, or patient-level values) could stand in for it.

Both teams assumed that the per-variant population-frequency columns in the mutation table (AFR_MAF, EUR_MAF, ExAC_AF_*) are annotations of variants and not per-patient ancestry estimates. That is correct, but neither team said so.
unused_evidence: data_mutations.txt holds per-variant population allele-frequency columns and matched-normal read counts (n_alt_count). These describe variants, not patients, so at most they give a weak germline proxy for ancestry. They cannot supply the income exposure, so they cannot change the label.
Clinical covariates (SMOKING, PSA, M_STAGE, DISEASE_EXTENT, GLEASON_SCORE, TMB) are not income measures. Both teams were right not to use them as proxies.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A searched only the first 6 lines of each file. A whole-file value search for geographic or income-like tokens was not reported.

Team B relied on a keyword grep plus manual review of the headers. This is adequate, because the clinical tables have only 9 patient and 14 sample columns and none of them concerns income or geography.
second_readings: Someone could read 'community-level average income' loosely and use a clinical proxy for it. The task's example of Not verifiable (the variable is absent) argues against that reading. No second reading of the quantity, group, scale or time turns the claim into a testable one.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed Not verifiable label highly. I checked the headers myself: the patient table has only age, race, smoking, PSA, M stage, vital status and disease extent, and no file holds an income, geographic or per-patient ancestry variable, so the exposure cannot be measured. No check I could ask for would plausibly change the label, so I am asking no questions.
